extracted.intended_audience: journalists, photo editors, media students, and the interested public concerned with media ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for evaluating the authenticity, provenance, and ethical publication of news photographs (when to publish, withdraw, or issue a 'picture kill'). Uses examples from the 2006 Lebanon conflict to illustrate failures and necessary newsroom policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image authenticity / no manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographs must not be manipulated to add drama or change the depicted events; manipulation that alters content is unacceptable (example: Adnan Hajj's doctored photographs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page describes 'image manipulation with excessive “production” to increase drama' and gives concrete examples (copying a single flare to appear as many missiles). When manipulation is discovered, images should be withdrawn and the author removed from the database. Emphasizes that 'Fake News had reached photographs.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Provenance and source verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify the origin and provenance of images and whether they were altered before publication (e.g., Reuters received images 'already manipulated' from a local photojournalist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Reuters response noted the image was received already manipulated from the photographer; this implies a need for checks on how an image was produced and who supplied it before distribution or front-page use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal / 'picture kill' policy
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations should have procedures to request that images not be used ('picture kill') and remove suspect images from their databases when manipulation is confirmed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reuters 'for the first time, issued a “picture kill”, a request that the image not be used by other media' and later 'withdraws the images and removes from its database all photographs by this author,' illustrating the remedy and policy action a newsroom should be prepared to take.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caption and factual accuracy verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Captions and accompanying text must be checked for factual accuracy and sequence — do not assert facts that the image does not reliably establish (example: a caption claiming bodies were still found when the same man later appears moving).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The New York Times example (caption about bodies still being found which was later contradicted by other photos of the same man moving) demonstrates the need to corroborate what a photograph purports to show before writing or publishing definitive captions or narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect and guard against staged/propagandistic imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Be alert to images or visual campaigns deliberately staged to change public perception or narrative (example: Hezbollah’s use of cleaned stuffed animals under rubble to suggest massacre).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents how a visual campaign 'changing the narrative to a massacre of innocent Lebanese citizens' used staged elements; guidance is to scrutinize images for staging, context, and possible propaganda intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional follow-up: stronger evaluation policies after failures
rubrics_metrics.description: When ethical breaches occur, news organizations should review and strengthen their image-evaluation policies and practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the incidents the Reuters Agency announced it 'would establish a more rigorous policy for evaluating images of the conflict in the Middle East,' indicating that institutional policy review and tightening is an expected response to manipulation incidents.
